project.title: Ledger Console
project.intro: Making financial interface rules inspectable in code
project.desc: A React and TypeScript concept ledger with reusable components, explicit money and refund rules, recovery states, and English/Arabic layouts. All transaction data is fictional.
project.insight: Financial interface quality depends on clear calculation, state and recovery contracts as much as the default screen.
project.nextMove: Validate the ledger tasks with users and confirm provider-owned money, access and refund rules before any production integration.
project.conclusion: A financial interface becomes easier to trust when money, state and recovery rules are inspectable; next, validate the tasks and provider-owned rules before production integration.
details: A single ledger page makes financial UI rules inspectable: 42 fictional transactions, six currencies and five transaction statuses. This is a personal implementation study, not a client product or a live payment service.

A polished table can still leave a reviewer unsure which currency an amount belongs to, how a fee affects a total, or what a refunded status actually returns. The page needed to explain money, status and recovery together.
Explicit currency Amounts show ISO currency codes. Sorting groups codes before comparing values; no FX conversion is implied.
Precision before totals Decimal midpoint values round away from zero into currency minor units. Totals add integer units, so display precision and calculation follow the same rule.

Refunds have their own breakdown The drawer separates original debit, principal returned, fee returned, refund credit and remaining net debit. Full and partial fixtures use an explicitly labelled demo policy that retains original fees.

A generator turns 78 base tokens into CSS properties and typed references. Shared controls and domain components cover filters, amounts, status badges, the transaction table and the focus-managed drawer. Dark and light modes share one component contract.

The visual treatment adapts selected components from a supplied Figma library. The ledger composition and interaction rules are implementation decisions for this concept; the documented mapping is not automatic Figma synchronization.

Network failure, permission denial and session expiry hide the transaction rows and provide local recovery. English and Arabic include the timeline; values use bidirectional isolation and explicit currency codes. Dates are consistently labelled UTC.
Core controls use 44px targets. Statuses combine words and icons. The drawer supports Tab containment, Escape and focus return. A narrow table scrolls inside its own labelled region.

The audit drove specific fixes: search placeholder contrast rose from 3.04:1 to 6.73:1 dark and 5.58:1 light, extra monetary precision was removed from fixtures, and blocked states and refund fields became explicit.

Seven automated money/refund tests and the TypeScript/Vite build pass. Browser checks cover filters, themes, drawer focus and recovery. These are implementation checks, not user-research findings, WCAG certification or measured business outcomes.

A production service would require server-owned financial records, authenticated permissions and provider-approved refund policies. Native-speaker review, screen-reader testing and task-based usability sessions remain future work. No funds move in this demo.

system.summary: Generated foundations, reusable UI and a local transaction model keep presentation and financial rules explicit.
system.flowSummary: Review a fictional record, narrow the list, inspect the breakdown and verify recovery without executing a payment.
system.evidenceSummary: The same ledger in dark/light themes, an explicit blocked state, and an Arabic partial-refund breakdown.
flow: Read the concept label and dataset scope.
Narrow by currency, status or reference.
Open the row to see amounts, fees and timeline.
Distinguish refund credit from remaining debit.
Preview a blocked state and restore the demo.
